```{r setup}
#| include: true
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)
library(cricketdata)

options(timeout = 300)

# Download the men's ODI ball-by-ball archive, then retain one match.
balls <- cricketdata::fetch_cricsheet(
  type = "bbb",
  gender = "male",
  competition = "odis"
) |>
  filter(match_id == 1384439) |>
  arrange(innings, actual_delivery) |>
  mutate(
    total_runs = runs_off_bat + extras,
    over = floor(ball) + 1L,
    # cricketdata imports unused character fields as "", not NA.
    is_wicket = !is.na(player_dismissed) &
      str_trim(player_dismissed) != ""
  ) |>
  group_by(innings) |>
  mutate(
    score_after_ball = cumsum(total_runs),
    over_position = floor(ball) +
      round((ball - floor(ball)) * 10) / 6
  ) |>
  ungroup()

overs <- balls |>
  group_by(innings, batting_team, over) |>
  summarise(
    over_runs = sum(total_runs),
    over_wickets = sum(is_wicket),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(innings, batting_team) |>
  mutate(
    score = cumsum(over_runs),
    wickets = cumsum(over_wickets)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

dismissals <- balls |>
  filter(is_wicket) |>
  select(innings, batting_team, over_position,
         score_after_ball, player_dismissed)

worm <- bind_rows(
  overs |>
    select(innings, batting_team, over, score, wickets),
  tibble(
    innings = c(1, 2),
    batting_team = c("India", "Australia"),
    over = 0L,
    score = 0,
    wickets = 0L
  )
) |>
  arrange(innings, over)

team_colours <- c(
  "Australia" = "#C58A00",
  "India" = "#0072B2"
)

theme_broadcast <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#D9E2E8", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      text = element_text(colour = "#142B3A"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "#344955"),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "#344955"),
      strip.text = element_text(colour = "#142B3A", face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#526773", hjust = 0)
    )
}
```

## 🎯 Objectives

By the end of this workshop, you will be able to:

* choose comparisons that answer a viewer's question during a match;
* reconstruct Manhattan and worm charts from ball-by-ball data; and
* show wickets without obscuring the pattern of runs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Preparation

Install the packages before class if needed:

``` r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "cricketdata"))
```
:::

## The broadcast brief

It is the **2023 Men's Cricket World Cup final** in Ahmedabad. India made
**240 all out**. Australia is chasing 241.

You are on the broadcast graphics team. Your audience wants to know:

> How does Australia's chase compare with India's innings at the same stage?

We will work from Cricsheet ball-by-ball data, accessed through the
`cricketdata` package. The match ID is `1384439`.

## What are we recreating?

These graphics have long appeared during cricket broadcasts. Look at how they
encode the match, rather than at the particular colours, logos or decoration.

### Manhattan chart

![](https://support.nvplay.com/hc/article_attachments/34464981203481){fig-alt="A cricket broadcast Manhattan chart with a pair of narrow bars for each over and small circles marking wickets." width="80%"}

Each bar shows the **runs scored in one over**, producing a skyline-like view
of changes in scoring intensity. The two teams can be shown in separate panels
or as adjacent bars. Circles mark overs in which wickets fell.

[Reference image: NV Play Streaming Overlay Control Panel.](https://support.nvplay.com/hc/en-gb/articles/34453205002393-Using-the-Streaming-Overlay-Control-Panel){.f4}

### Worm chart

![](https://cricamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/JamTkr-Worm-Screen-768x432.jpg){fig-alt="A cricket television worm chart comparing two teams with cumulative-run lines and circular wicket markers." width="80%"}

Each line shows **cumulative runs as the innings progresses**. A steeper section
means faster scoring; the relative height of the lines compares the teams at
the same stage. Circles show where wickets interrupted each innings.

[Reference image: 2018 Caribbean Premier League broadcast, via CricAmerica.](https://cricamerica.com/understanding-the-tv-screen/){.f4}

## 1. Read the moment before drawing (5 minutes)

After ten overs:

| Team | Score | Run rate | Match situation |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| India | 80/2 | 8.00 | setting the target |
| Australia | 60/3 | 6.00 | needs 181 from 240 balls (4.53 per over) |

Discuss with a partner:

1. Which comparison would a viewer care about: score, wickets, run rate, or
   required run rate?
2. Is Australia “behind” after ten overs? Write a one-sentence answer.
3. Which quantities should be encoded visually, and which belong in text?

::: {.unilur-solution}
## Discussion notes

Australia is 20 runs behind India's score at the same stage and has lost one
more wicket. However, it is scoring faster than the required rate. “Behind” is
therefore ambiguous: the answer depends on whether we mean comparative score,
resources remaining, or progress towards the target.

This is a useful reason not to force score, wickets and rates onto one set of
axes. Show the dominant comparison visually and use a direct label or short
annotation for the other context.
:::

## 2. Design a live checkpoint graphic (8 minutes)

Choose `checkpoint <- 10`, `20` or `30`. The code below creates the two rows
available to the graphics producer at that moment.

```{r checkpoint-data}
#| echo: true
checkpoint <- 10

snapshot <- overs |>
  filter(over == checkpoint) |>
  mutate(label = paste(score, "/", wickets))

snapshot
```

On paper, or in `ggplot2`, design a compact comparison that could appear
between overs. It must:

* make the runs easy to compare;
* retain the wicket context;
* say that both teams are being compared after the same number of overs; and
* use direct labels rather than making the viewer search a legend.

Swap checkpoint values. Does the headline remain true?

::: {.unilur-solution}
## One possible checkpoint graphic

```{r checkpoint-solution}
checkpoint <- 10

snapshot <- overs |>
  filter(over == checkpoint) |>
  mutate(
    label = paste(score, "/", wickets),
    batting_team = fct_reorder(batting_team, score)
  )

ggplot(snapshot, aes(score, batting_team, fill = batting_team)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.58) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    hjust = 1.05,
    colour = "#071A2B",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = team_colours) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    x = "Runs", y = NULL,
    title = paste("After", checkpoint, "overs"),
    subtitle = "Both innings at the same stage"
  ) +
  theme_broadcast()
```

At 20 overs India still leads, 115/3 to 104/3. At 30 overs the story changes:
Australia leads 167/3 to 152/4. A graphic designed for a live broadcast needs
to remain truthful as the match state changes; a fixed takeaway title may not.
:::

## 3. Rebuild the Manhattan chart (12 minutes)

A Manhattan chart uses bar height to show runs scored in each over. Start with
the skeleton below.

```{r manhattan-starter}
#| eval: false
ggplot(overs, aes(over, over_runs, fill = batting_team)) +
  # Add one bar per over
  # Separate the innings so bars never hide one another
  # Add a mark when over_wickets is greater than zero
  scale_fill_manual(values = team_colours) +
  labs(
    x = "Over", y = "Runs in over",
    title = "Where did each innings accelerate?"
  ) +
  theme_broadcast()
```

Before coding, decide:

1. Should the two innings be overlaid, dodged or placed in separate panels?
2. Where can a wicket marker go without being mistaken for more runs?
3. What does this chart reveal that the ten-over checkpoint cannot?

::: {.unilur-solution}
## Manhattan solution

### Faceted version

```{r manhattan-solution}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(overs, aes(over, over_runs, fill = batting_team)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.86) +
  geom_point(
    data = ~ filter(.x, over_wickets > 0),
    aes(y = over_runs + 1.2),
    shape = 21,
    stroke = 0.7,
    size = 2.6,
    colour = "#142B3A"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ batting_team, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = team_colours) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    x = "Over", y = "Runs in over",
    title = "Australia kept the chase moving after an early collapse",
    subtitle = "India's scoring slowed sharply after the powerplay",
    caption = "Dots mark overs in which a wicket fell. Source: Cricsheet via cricketdata."
  ) +
  theme_broadcast()
```

Faceting preserves a common horizontal and vertical scale while avoiding
occlusion. Each wicket dot sits just above its bar, so it is associated with an
over but cannot be read as part of the bar's magnitude.

### Dodged version

```{r manhattan-solution-dodged}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
dodge_width <- 0.86

dodged_overs <- overs |>
  select(batting_team, over, over_runs, over_wickets) |>
  complete(
    over = 1:50,
    batting_team = c("Australia", "India")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    over_wickets = replace_na(over_wickets, 0L),
    over_block = factor(
      if_else(over <= 25, "Overs 1–25", "Overs 26–50"),
      levels = c("Overs 1–25", "Overs 26–50")
    )
  )

dodge <- position_dodge2(
  width = dodge_width,
  preserve = "single",
  padding = 0.08
)

ggplot(dodged_overs, aes(over, over_runs, fill = batting_team)) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.8,
    position = dodge,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      y = if_else(over_wickets > 0, over_runs + 1.2, NA_real_)
    ),
    position = dodge,
    shape = 21,
    stroke = 0.7,
    size = 2.6,
    colour = "#142B3A",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ over_block, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = team_colours, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    x = "Over", y = "Runs in over",
    title = "Australia kept the chase moving after an early collapse",
    subtitle = "India's scoring slowed sharply after the powerplay",
    caption = "Dots mark overs in which a wicket fell. Source: Cricsheet via cricketdata."
  ) +
  theme_broadcast() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )
```

The same `position_dodge2()` specification is applied to both geoms. The point
layer retains every team–over row while assigning `NA` to non-wicket heights;
this lets `ggplot2` calculate the same team offset before it removes the
unneeded points. `preserve = "single"` prevents India's bars from becoming
wider after Australia's innings ends. Splitting the match into two 25-over
panels makes the paired bars easier to distinguish, while the innings-faceted
version gives each team more room.
:::

## 4. Rebuild the worm chart (12 minutes)

A worm chart shows cumulative runs against overs. Use `worm` for the lines and
`dismissals` for the wicket events.

```{r worm-starter}
#| eval: false
ggplot(worm, aes(over, score, colour = batting_team)) +
  # Add one line for each batting team
  # Add an offset circle for each row in the dismissals data frame
  # Directly label each line
  scale_colour_manual(values = team_colours) +
  labs(
    x = "Overs", y = "Runs",
    title = "When did Australia's chase move ahead?"
  ) +
  theme_broadcast()
```

Your wicket layer will need its own mappings:

``` r
aes(
  x = over,
  y = score,
  fill = batting_team,
  colour = batting_team
)
```

Ask another pair to read your chart. Can they identify the early danger, the
crossover and the winning moment without you explaining them?

::: {.unilur-solution}
## Worm solution

```{r worm-solution}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(worm, aes(over, score, colour = batting_team)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.35) +
  geom_point(
    data = dismissals,
    aes(
      x = over_position,
      y = score_after_ball + 4,
      fill = batting_team
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21,
    size = 2.8,
    stroke = 0.7,
    colour = "#142B3A"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 241,
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#7A8D99"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 49.5, y = 246,
    label = "Target: 241", hjust = 1,
    colour = "#344955", size = 3.7
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = team_colours, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = team_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    x = "Overs", y = "Cumulative runs",
    title = "Australia recovered from 47/3 to overhaul India's 240",
    subtitle = "A 192-run partnership changed the shape of the chase",
    caption = "Source: Cricsheet via cricketdata."
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.5))
  ) +
  theme_broadcast() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.13, 0.82),
    legend.background = element_rect(
      fill = scales::alpha("white", 0.92),
      colour = "#B8C5CC"
    ),
    legend.text = element_text(colour = "#142B3A", face = "bold"),
    legend.margin = margin(5, 8, 5, 8)
  )
```

The line makes the changing run-rate visible through its slope. Wickets are
events rather than magnitudes, so points are a better encoding than a second
axis. The worm reveals the early collapse and later crossover more clearly than
the Manhattan chart; the Manhattan chart better reveals volatile individual
overs.
:::

## 5. Broadcast review (8 minutes)

Choose either your Manhattan or worm chart. Give it a final editorial pass:

1. Write a takeaway title of no more than 14 words.
2. Add a subtitle that supplies essential match context rather than repeating
   the title.
3. Check that colour is not the only way to identify wickets or teams.
4. Remove one element that does not help a viewer answer the broadcast question.
5. Write one sentence describing what your graphic still cannot tell us.

::: {.callout-note}
## Fast finisher: freeze the broadcast

Create the worm as it would have appeared after 10, 20 or 30 overs of the chase.
Filter both innings to that checkpoint and rewrite the title for what was known
**at that moment**. Do not use knowledge of the final result.
:::

::: {.unilur-solution}
## Instructor notes

Suggested running time is 5 + 8 + 12 + 12 + 8 minutes, with five minutes for
transitions or a whole-class comparison of designs.

The 2023 World Cup final is useful because the encodings tell complementary
stories. India led by 20 runs after ten overs, but Australia was already above
the required rate. Australia moved ahead between overs 20 and 30 and won at
241/4 after 43 overs. Their first three wickets make the chase look precarious;
the long wicket-free section then becomes the dominant feature of the worm.

A defensible limitation is that neither chart attributes the change to batting,
bowling, pitch conditions or tactics. Both show what happened, not why it
happened.
:::

## Supplied data-preparation code

Keep this code for reference. You do **not** need to recreate it during the
workshop.

```{r supplied-code}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(cricketdata)

balls <- cricketdata::fetch_cricsheet(
  type = "bbb",
  gender = "male",
  competition = "odis"
) |>
  filter(match_id == 1384439) |>
  arrange(innings, actual_delivery) |>
  mutate(
    total_runs = runs_off_bat + extras,
    over = floor(ball) + 1L,
    # Blank dismissal fields are empty strings in cricketdata's CSV import.
    is_wicket = !is.na(player_dismissed) &
      str_trim(player_dismissed) != ""
  ) |>
  group_by(innings) |>
  mutate(
    score_after_ball = cumsum(total_runs),
    over_position = floor(ball) +
      round((ball - floor(ball)) * 10) / 6
  ) |>
  ungroup()

overs <- balls |>
  group_by(innings, batting_team, over) |>
  summarise(
    over_runs = sum(total_runs),
    over_wickets = sum(is_wicket),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(innings, batting_team) |>
  mutate(
    score = cumsum(over_runs),
    wickets = cumsum(over_wickets)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

dismissals <- balls |>
  filter(is_wicket) |>
  select(innings, batting_team, over_position,
         score_after_ball, player_dismissed)

worm <- bind_rows(
  overs |>
    select(innings, batting_team, over, score, wickets),
  tibble(
    innings = c(1, 2),
    batting_team = c("India", "Australia"),
    over = 0L,
    score = 0,
    wickets = 0L
  )
) |>
  arrange(innings, over)
```

Data: [Cricsheet](https://cricsheet.org/) via the
[`cricketdata`](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/cricketdata/) R package.
Match: India v Australia, ICC Men's Cricket World Cup final, 19 November 2023.
